notes.bp: A community can communicate by whistling, so a listener must know how spoken vowel and stress distinctions survive when the sound source changes.
notes.wh: Whistling removes many speech cues and concentrates information in pitch and intensity, so a spoken-language assumption may misidentify what remains contrastive.
notes.naive: Assume every spoken vowel and stress cue must have the same acoustic realization in the whistle register.
notes.ap: Compare matched minimal pairs in spoken and whistled Greek and identify which vowel and stress contrasts are carried by F0, intensity, or neither.
notes.mech: Participants produce five Greek vowel qualities in Sfyria whistling and spoken Greek; acoustic contrasts are compared for stressed and unstressed forms.
notes.math: The representation changes with the communication channel: F0 and intensity are alternative carriers of phonological contrast, and a missing cue is itself evidence.
notes.ww: All five vowel qualities remain distinct in the whistled register, but a whistled stress correlate is not found for /i/, possibly because front vowels are already highly intense.
notes.limits: The Sfyria community, participants, register, minimal pairs, and acoustic cues bound the result; a ceiling interpretation and cross-language generalization remain open.
notes.title: Stress in Spoken and Whistled Greek

notes.bp: One emotion recognizer should serve several languages without letting the largest language erase smaller languages or their emotion patterns.
notes.wh: Languages differ in acoustic and linguistic cues, and one teacher model may be strong in one language but transfer the wrong priorities to another.
notes.naive: Train one multilingual model directly or average teacher predictions without identifying which language produced the speech.
notes.ap: Use separate monolingual teachers and a language-aware distillation process to teach one student while preserving language-specific evidence.
notes.mech: Wav2vec2 teachers for English, Finnish, and French are distilled into one multilingual student and evaluated by emotion recall per language and class.
notes.math: The student is a shared model with language-conditioned supervision; weighted and unweighted recall expose both overall performance and class imbalance.
notes.ww: The student reports weighted recall 72.9 on English and unweighted recall 63.4 on Finnish, with stronger gains for sad and neutral than anger and happiness.
notes.limits: Languages, emotion labels, teacher quality, class balance, and recall metrics bound the claim; multilingual transfer does not prove equal performance or culturally valid emotion categories.
notes.title: Multi-Teacher Language-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Multilingual Speech Emotion Recognition

notes.bp: A physical vocal-tract replica should reveal the resonances of a modeled vowel, but the printed walls can vibrate and create false peaks and gaps.
notes.wh: The measurement apparatus can confuse sound transmitted through the model body with sound traveling through the intended tract cavity.
notes.naive: Trust the measured transfer function or change only the acoustic excitation while ignoring the replica's structural vibration.
notes.ap: Dampen or mechanically constrain the replica and test whether the expected resonances become cleaner and more repeatable.
notes.mech: Ten axisymmetric 3D-printed vowel tubes are measured with reciprocity; sound-absorbing fabric and sand embedding are compared as artifact-reduction methods.
notes.math: The transfer function is a physical measurement shaped by both air paths and solid-body vibration; artifact reduction is tested through resonance structure and repeatability.
notes.ww: Both coverings reduce spurious poles and zeros and improve repeatability of the measured transfer functions.
notes.limits: Printed geometries, ten vowels, materials, reciprocity setup, and repeatability metric bound the claim; improved measurement does not prove the replica matches a human tract.
notes.title: Influence of wall coverings of 3D-printed vocal tract models on measured transfer functions

notes.bp: Two different tongue and lip gestures may produce similar formant changes, so a listener or analyst cannot infer articulation from one acoustic cue alone.
notes.wh: Labialization and pharyngealization modify different parts of the tract but can both lower F2, making a shared acoustic effect look like a shared gesture.
notes.naive: Treat a low F2 as proof of one particular secondary articulation.
notes.ap: Compare adjacent-vowel formants across both articulations, vowel qualities, and speakers, then identify which formants preserve their difference.
notes.mech: Thirty-five Tashlhiyt speakers produce VCV logatomes with /i, a, u/ and labialized or pharyngealized consonants; F1 and F2 patterns are compared.
notes.math: The mapping is many-to-one: F2 can reveal a broad acoustic effect while F1 and vowel context retain articulatory distinctions.
notes.ww: Both articulations show similar F2 effects, strongest for /i/ and then /a/, while differences depend on F1 and vowel quality.
notes.limits: The language, speakers, logatomes, adjacent vowels, and formant measures bound the result; formants alone cannot identify every articulatory gesture.
notes.title: Equivalence and differences: Formant patterns of labialization and pharyngealization in Tashlhiyt

notes.bp: A recognizer must process long recordings without making attention cost grow too quickly or forgetting what happened earlier.
notes.wh: Short-form transformer success does not guarantee tractable long-form decoding, and a model with local efficiency may lose useful distant context.
notes.naive: Apply ordinary quadratic self-attention to the entire recording or split it into chunks and discard cross-chunk memory.
notes.ap: Compare linear-time sequence architectures and add a non-trained nearest-neighbor memory that retrieves useful earlier representations during inference.
notes.mech: Fastformer, SummaryMixing, BiMamba, and E-Branchformer variants are evaluated on a new LibriHeavy long-form benchmark; KNN-MAN is added to encoder-decoder models.
notes.math: Long-form recognition is a time-scale and memory problem: architecture controls cost while retrieval supplies selected history; WER across duration scales tests the tradeoff.
notes.ww: The paper reports a reduction from 18.8% to 17.5% WER on its LibriSpeech long-form test-clean example with BiMamba and KNN-MAN.
notes.limits: Benchmark construction, duration distribution, memory retrieval, architectures, and WER bound the result; a single long-form corpus does not establish general conversation robustness.
notes.title: Exploring Linear Variant Transformers and k-NN Memory Inference for Long-Form ASR

notes.bp: A speech language model should generate high-quality audio quickly, but autoregressive generation must produce many codec tokens for each second of speech.
notes.wh: A high-rate codec can preserve detail while making training and inference slow; lowering the rate can destroy quality or causal timing.
notes.naive: Use a high-frame-rate codec and accept the step count, or reduce frames without testing which bitrate and causality choices caused the quality loss.
notes.ap: Measure the separate effects of frame rate, bitrate, and causality, then design a codec with a low frame rate that still reconstructs speech well.
notes.mech: NanoCodec is evaluated through codec ablations and compared across bitrate ranges, targeting 12.5 frames per second for speech LLM training and inference.
notes.math: The codec converts a continuous waveform into fewer discrete generation steps; reconstruction quality and rate expose the speed-quality boundary.
notes.ww: The paper reports high-quality compression at 12.5 FPS and competitive performance across tested bitrates.
notes.limits: Codec architecture, audio data, bitrate, causality, quality metric, and hardware bound the result; low frame rate alone does not prove low end-to-end latency.
notes.title: NanoCodec: Towards High-Quality Ultra Fast Speech LLM Inference

notes.bp: A person with dysarthria may know the intended words but produce speech that listeners cannot understand; reconstruction should improve clarity without replacing the person's voice.
notes.wh: Content is hard to recover from atypical acoustics, while a system that focuses only on clarity can erase speaker identity.
notes.naive: Train a generic speech enhancer or normalize the voice toward an average speaker.
notes.ap: Separate content recovery from identity preservation and generate a clearer signal in a latent space conditioned on both.
notes.mech: DiffDSR uses a self-supervised speech content encoder, an in-context speaker identity encoder, and a latent diffusion generator on UASpeech.
notes.math: The system has two constraints—recover phoneme content and retain speaker identity—so intelligibility and speaker similarity must be evaluated separately.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved speech intelligibility and speaker similarity over prior dysarthric speech reconstruction methods on UASpeech.
notes.limits: UASpeech, speaker identities, dysarthria types, reconstruction target, and metrics bound the claim; improved similarity and intelligibility are not clinical validation or authorship proof.
notes.title: DiffDSR: Dysarthric Speech Reconstruction Using Latent Diffusion Model

notes.bp: A large self-supervised speech model may be useful but too expensive to store or run, so a smaller student must retain the teacher's reusable speech knowledge.
notes.wh: Layer-by-layer imitation adds alignment machinery and can force the student to copy the teacher's structure rather than its learning objective.
notes.naive: Compress each teacher layer with a separate matching module or simply shrink the network and accept lost representations.
notes.ap: Replace the HuBERT teacher with a smaller student trained directly under HuBERT's iterative self-supervised objective.
notes.mech: DiceHuBERT distills HuBERT using the same self-supervised objective and evaluates the compact model on phoneme recognition, ASR, and SUPERB tasks.
notes.math: The student learns the task's predictive structure instead of matching every hidden layer; downstream performance measures retained usefulness across tasks.
notes.ww: The paper reports over 21% improvement in phoneme recognition and over 14% in ASR relative to existing distillation methods, with competitive multi-task results.
notes.limits: Teacher/student sizes, SUPERB tasks, training data, and comparison baselines bound the result; benchmark transfer does not establish equal behavior under every deployment constraint.
notes.title: DiceHuBERT: Distilling HuBERT with a Self-Supervised Learning Objective
